title: Check if a string is a palindrome (two-pointer, skip non-alphanumeric).
shortTitle: Check If a String Is a Palindrome — Two-Pointer, Skip Non-Alphanumeric

s1_definition.profdef: A palindrome check determines whether a string reads the same forward and backward, typically ignoring case and non-alphanumeric characters. The optimal solution uses two pointers from both ends that skip over any non-alphanumeric character, compare the remaining characters case-insensitively, and return false on the first mismatch. It runs in linear time with constant extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India validates certain vanity account nicknames that are supposed to be symmetric, like a mirror, ignoring spaces, punctuation, and capitalization. Two fingers start at the first and last meaningful characters. If either lands on a space or a symbol, that finger steps past it. Then the two meaningful characters are compared ignoring case; if they ever differ, it is not symmetric; if the fingers meet in the middle without a mismatch, it is.
s1_definition.oneliner: Walk two pointers inward, skip non-alphanumeric characters, and compare case-insensitively until they meet.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A palindrome check determines whether a string reads the same forward and backward, typically ignoring case and non-alphanumeric characters. The optimal solution uses two pointers from both ends that skip over any non-alphanumeric character, compare the remaining characters case-insensitively, and return false on the first mismatch. It runs in linear time with constant extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India validates certain vanity account nicknames that are supposed to be symmetric, like a mirror, ignoring spaces, punctuation, and capitalization. Two fingers start at the first and last meaningful characters. If either lands on a space or a symbol, that finger steps past it. Then the two meaningful characters are compared ignoring case; if they ever differ, it is not symmetric; if the fingers meet in the middle without a mismatch, it is.

**One line to remember:** Walk two pointers inward, skip non-alphanumeric characters, and compare case-insensitively until they meet.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive approach cleans the string first, removing non-alphanumeric characters and lowercasing, then reverses it and compares. That works but allocates extra strings. The two-pointer approach avoids all that allocation by comparing in place on the original string, skipping unwanted characters as it goes.

You start a left pointer at index zero and a right pointer at the last index. In a loop that runs while left is less than right, you first advance the left pointer forward while it points at a non-alphanumeric character and is still left of right, and similarly move the right pointer backward while it points at a non-alphanumeric character and is still right of left. Now both pointers are on alphanumeric characters. You compare them case-insensitively, usually by lowercasing both, and if they differ you return false immediately. If they match, you move both pointers inward by one and continue.

Skipping non-alphanumeric characters inside the loop, rather than pre-cleaning, is what keeps the space constant. The character classification uses a helper such as Character.isLetterOrDigit, and the case-insensitive comparison uses Character.toLowerCase on both sides. The early return on the first mismatch is what makes typical inputs fast, since a non-palindrome often fails near the ends.

A senior point is the guard conditions on the skip loops. Each skip loop must also check that left is still less than right, otherwise for a string of only punctuation the pointers could run past each other and index out of bounds. By keeping the left-less-than-right guard in both the outer loop and the inner skip loops, the algorithm safely handles strings that are entirely non-alphanumeric, which count as palindromes because they contain no meaningful characters to contradict symmetry.

Another senior point is locale and Unicode in case folding. Character.toLowerCase is fine for ASCII, but full Unicode case folding can be locale-sensitive, for example the Turkish dotless i. For bank nicknames restricted to ASCII letters and digits this does not bite, but I mention it because a naive lowercase can misbehave in some locales, and a robust internationalized version would use a locale-aware normalization.

A small finance-domain example: `while(l<r){ while(l<r && !isLetterOrDigit(s.charAt(l))) l++; while(l<r && !isLetterOrDigit(s.charAt(r))) r--; if(toLowerCase(s.charAt(l))!=toLowerCase(s.charAt(r))) return false; l++; r--; } return true;` validates a nickname in place.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India lets customers set a vanity nickname on an account, and a validation rule flags whether the nickname is a palindrome, reading the same both ways, ignoring spaces, punctuation, and case, for a themed rewards promotion. The check runs on every nickname submission so it must be fast and allocation-light. A two-pointer palindrome check with skipping is exactly this.

This is exactly how a palindrome check works in Java — two pointers inward that skip non-alphanumeric characters and compare case-insensitively.

Problem 2 — Nicknames can contain spaces, commas, and mixed case, and some are entirely punctuation which should count as a palindrome, and the check must never index out of bounds. This shows the skip-with-guard logic and the all-punctuation edge case.

What the code will do: a `NicknameValidator` with `isPalindrome(String nickname)` using two pointers that skip non-alphanumeric characters with proper guards. The demo validates several nicknames.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the nickname `A man, a plan, a canal: Panama`.

Step 1: the left pointer starts at the first character `A`, the right pointer at the last character `a`. Both are alphanumeric, so no skipping is needed. We lowercase both to `a` and `a`; they match, so we move inward.

Step 2: the left pointer now points at a space, which is non-alphanumeric, so the left skip loop advances it to the next letter `m`. The right pointer points at `m` as well after any needed skipping. We compare `m` and `m`; they match, move inward.

Step 3: as the pointers continue, every space, comma, and colon is skipped by the inner loops, and only the letters are compared. The comparison sequence is the letters of amanaplanacanalpanama read from both ends, which match symmetrically at every step.

Step 4: eventually the pointers meet in the middle without any mismatch, so the outer loop ends and we return true. The punctuation and spaces never caused a false mismatch because they were skipped rather than compared.

Step 5: for `Rajesh`, the first comparison is `r` against `h`, which already differ, so we return false immediately. For the all-punctuation `.,`, both skip loops advance the pointers until they cross without ever comparing a letter, so the outer loop ends with true, correctly treating a string with no meaningful characters as a palindrome.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T20:10:00Z INFO 'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama' IS a palindrome
2026-10-26T20:10:00Z INFO Result = true
2026-10-26T20:10:00Z INFO 'Rajesh' is NOT a palindrome
2026-10-26T20:10:00Z INFO Result = false
2026-10-26T20:10:00Z INFO '.,' IS a palindrome
2026-10-26T20:10:00Z INFO Result = true
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"  left=0 right=end
    │
    ▼
  while left<right: skip non-alnum both sides; compare lowercase
    │ 'a'=='a' ✓ move in
    │ skip ' ' ',' etc; 'm'=='m' ✓
    │ ... all letters match symmetrically
    │ pointers meet, no mismatch
    ▼
  true   ("Rajesh" → 'r'!='h' → false early)
    ▼
  Output: palindrome yes/no
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A palindrome check decides whether a string reads the same forward and backward, usually ignoring case and non-alphanumeric characters, and I solve it with two pointers in linear time and constant space without pre-cleaning the string. A left pointer starts at the front and a right pointer at the back, and in each iteration I first skip past any non-alphanumeric character on each side, then compare the two meaningful characters case-insensitively, returning false immediately on the first mismatch.

Skipping the unwanted characters inside the loop rather than building a cleaned copy first is what keeps the space constant, and the early return on a mismatch makes typical non-palindromes fast because they often fail right near the ends. I classify characters with isLetterOrDigit and fold case with toLowerCase on both sides so punctuation, spaces, and capitalization never cause a false mismatch.

The detail I always get right is the guard on the skip loops. Each inner skip must also check that the left pointer is still less than the right, otherwise a string of only punctuation would run the pointers past each other and index out of bounds. With that guard, an all-punctuation string correctly returns true, since it has no meaningful characters to break symmetry. I also note that full Unicode case folding can be locale-sensitive, which matters for internationalized input though not for ASCII nicknames.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to validate vanity account nicknames for a rewards promotion, flagging the ones that read the same both ways while ignoring spaces, punctuation, and case, running on every submission with no extra allocation. Explaining the in-loop skipping, the guarded pointers, the early mismatch exit, and the case-folding caveat shows the interviewer that I handle the real messy-input version of this problem, not just the clean textbook one.
